q: The technician switches on the chartplotter, waits for the fix, shows you this and turns to the VHF. What do you ask before he moves on?
a: Whether the card covers the whole cruising ground, and how old the chart is
o: Nothing — a plotter with a fix is a working plotter
Whether the screen can be dimmed for night passages
Whether the plotter also drives the autopilot
why: Check the chart covers everywhere you will go and ask its edition: an old card misses new marinas, moles and shoals.

q: At the berth the instruments show this, and the base's harbour plan gives 3.0 m here. What has happened?
a: The sounder is set to feet — 9.8 ft is 3.0 m; switch the units to metres
o: The transducer is fouled — the reading is random
It shows the depth at the harbour mouth, not the berth
The offset is set below the keel — add the draught
why: 9.8 ft = 3.0 m. Greek and Croatian charts are in metres: set depth to metres and distance to nautical miles before you sail.

lines: Harbour plan: 3.0 m at the berth

q: You check the sounder against the harbour plan at the berth. How much water is under the keel right now?
a: About 1.6 m — the sounder reads from the transducer, not from the keel
o: 3.3 m — the reading is already the water below the keel
1.4 m — take the draught off the reading
3.5 m — the plan is right and the sounder is 0.2 m out
why: No offset: the reading is depth below the transducer, 0.2 m under the surface here. Below the keel: 3.5 − 1.9 ≈ 1.6 m.

lines: Harbour plan: 3.5 m at the berth

q: Going through the plotter, the technician points at the MOB key and moves on. What do you do with it?
a: Ask him to show how it marks and how it clears, then brief the crew on it
o: Leave it — a casualty is recovered by eye, not from a screen
Note that it is the red button on the VHF handset
Press and hold it now to test the DSC distress alert
why: MOB on the plotter drops a waypoint and shows bearing and distance back; the crew must know where it is before it is needed.

q: On the test run outside the harbour the display shows this. What do you write on the check-in form?
a: Log reads zero — paddle wheel fouled; ask the base to clear it
o: GPS fault — SOG shows a speed with no log input
Nothing — SOG from the plotter does for the week
Plotter has lost its fix — reboot it at the berth
why: A fouled paddle wheel reads 0; the base pulls and cleans it in the harbour. Note it: speed through the water feeds true wind and the log book.

q: A steady breeze blows across the marina and the burgee flies at the masthead, yet the instruments show this. What do you do?
a: Note it — masthead unit dead; ask the base to look at it before you leave
o: Accept it — the wind shows only once the boat is sailing
Go up in the bosun's chair and check the sensor yourself
Tap the display — it needs some minutes to warm up
why: The wind instrument should show direction and speed at the berth; a dead one is logged and fixed by the base, not by you aloft.

q: This is the whole of the technician's autopilot briefing. What do you do?
a: Ask to see Standby, a course change and the alarms, and try it on the test run
o: Accept it — AUTO is the only button you will need
Read the manual the first time you need it at sea
Leave it switched off and hand-steer for the week
why: Know how to engage, disengage and what the alarm means before you rely on it — and never in harbours or close quarters.

fig.title: Autopilot
lines: Not tried on the test run

q: The technician finishes his radio check and leaves the set like this. What do you set before leaving the berth?
a: Channel 16, dual watch on the base's working channel, squelch just above the hiss
o: Leave 72 — the base calls you on it all week
Channel 16 with squelch fully up to keep it quiet
Channel 16 alone — dual watch drains the battery
why: Under way you keep a watch on 16; dual watch adds the working channel. Squelch fully up mutes weak calls.

q: The technician asks you to do the radio check yourself. How do you make the call?
a: Call the base on its working channel with the boat's name and ask for a readability report
o: Call the base on channel 16 — a check must be heard by all
Send a DSC test call to the base on channel 70
Call the coastguard on channel 16 and ask for a check
why: Radio checks go on a working channel, not on 16, which is kept for distress, safety and calling.

q: You open the DSC page of the fixed VHF and look at the front of the set. What do you do?
a: Ask for the boat's MMSI to be programmed and the cover replaced before you sign
o: Enter the MMSI printed on your own SRC certificate
Program the base's phone number in as the MMSI
Ignore it — DSC is for ships, not charter yachts
why: Without the ship's MMSI a DSC alert carries no identity; the cover prevents false alerts. Both are the base's job.

q: The inventory lists a handheld VHF. This is what you find in the chart-table drawer. What do you do?
a: Ask for the charger and a full charge before you sign, and note it on the form
o: Leave it — the fixed set is the one that matters
Take it as it is — one bar lasts a week on standby
Have it struck off the inventory to avoid a deposit claim
why: The handheld is the radio for the dinghy and the liferaft; flat and without a charger it is useless. Have it charged and listed.

q: The plotter's AIS page shows the harbour traffic. What do you ask the technician?
a: Whether it is receive-only or a transponder — can the ferries see you?
o: Whether it shows yachts as well as ships
Whether the targets also appear on the VHF screen
Whether the CPA alarm can be switched off at night
why: A receiver shows others to you; only a transponder shows you to them. Know which before you cross a ferry route at night.

q: On the test run, in flat water with no current, you compare the steering compass with the plotter's course over the ground. What do you do?
a: Look for a phone or speaker by the binnacle, then note the deviation that remains
o: Set the plotter to magnetic north so that the two agree
Accept 8° — that is the variation in the Ionian
Swing the compass yourself before leaving the harbour
why: Compass 090° + 3°E variation = 093° true; the other 5° is deviation — often a phone on the binnacle. Note it; the plotter steers by GPS.

q: You tick the navigation kit off against the inventory. What do you ask the base for?
a: A pilot book of the area and a current chart, before you sign
o: Nothing — the chartplotter replaces all of it
A second pair of binoculars for the crew
A tide table and a set of tidal-stream atlases
why: Paper chart and pilot book are the backup and the harbour detail the plotter lacks; an old chart misses new moles and depths.

q: In the chart-table drawer you find this. The technician says nobody uses it any more. What do you do with it during the week?
a: Keep it: each day's departure and arrival, positions and times, engine hours, weather, anything that broke
o: Leave it — the plotter's track is the boat's record
Fill it in on Friday evening from memory before the check-out
Use it only if the port police ask to see a log
why: The log is your record for the base, the insurer and the port police: when you were where, the engine hours, the damage you reported.

fig.title: Log book
lines: Columns: time, position, course, log, wind, engine hours
Pencil on a string, half the pages left

q: Your mate, who has no radio certificate, asks whether she may use the VHF during the week. What do you tell her?
a: Yes, under your supervision as the certificated operator — and anyone may call in distress
o: No — only the holder of the SRC may touch the set
Yes, freely — the boat's ship licence covers the crew
Only the handheld, never the fixed DSC set
why: The ship licence covers the set; an SRC holder is in charge of it and crew operate under supervision. Distress may be sent by anyone.
ref: VHF licence — operator and ship station

q: The base's briefing has a weather page. What do you take from it when you plan the week?
a: Sail early, reef before the afternoon, allow for the current in the channel
o: Ignore tide and current — there is none in the Med
Plan the long legs for the afternoon, when the wind is up
Stay in the marina on every day the Meltemi blows
why: The Med has little tide, but wind-driven currents in channels are real; the Meltemi builds by afternoon, so passages go early.

q: You switch the plotter on at the berth in the base and it shows this. What do you do?
a: Treat it as a stale fix — wait for a lock, then check the position against the berth
o: Enter a position correction so the boat sits on the berth
Assume the base moved the boat overnight
Accept it — plotters are good to about half a mile
why: Until it has satellites the plotter shows the last stored position. Check the fix time and that the boat sits on its berth before trusting it.
ref: Check-in: GPS fix at the berth

fig.note: Plotter screen at the berth, Sat 17:00

q: You set up the sounder's shallow-water alarm from these figures. What do you set it to?
a: About 3 m — the keel touches at 1.7 m on this sounder, plus a margin
o: 1.0 m as found — the alarm is about the hull, not the keel
2.1 m — the draught, exactly
5 m — anything closer is a nuisance in Greek bays
why: The keel touches when the sounder reads 2.1 − 0.4 = 1.7 m; add a metre or so of margin. Set it, and tell the crew what the alarm means.

q: The depth sounder is blank and the base answers as shown. What do you do?
a: Have it written on the form as unserviceable and ask for a fix or a lead line before you sail
o: Sail anyway — the Ionian is deep and you know the bays
Refuse the boat and demand the deposit back
Sign now and raise it by phone with the base on Monday
why: A dead instrument is noted at hand-over so it is not charged to you, and a boat without depth is not fit to anchor: push for a fix.
